case_info.scenario: A man in his 30s presented with an approximately 6-month history of asymptomatic plaques on the dorsal bilateral first digits of the feet. He had no relevant medical history or any known inciting factors. Physical examination demonstrated thick yellow to brown plaques overlying the interphalangeal joints of both first digits of the feet (Figure, A). A combination of urea cream, 20%, and clobetasol ointment, 0.05%, applied twice daily to the affected area for approximately 4 weeks yielded no improvement. At a follow-up visit, a tangential shave biopsy specimen was taken from the right dorsal first digit toe (Figure, B).
case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of yellow-brown plaques on the dorsal bilateral first digits of the feet, with prominent scale and a healing biopsy site on the right great toe. Plaques are centered on the interphalangeal joint, potentially an area of high friction. B, Histopathologic examination showed large cells with small, round, dark blue central nuclei and abundant light pink cytoplasm scattered within the epidermis.
case_info.explanation: The shave biopsy findings revealed numerous keratinocytes with abundant pink cytoplasm, scattered at all levels of the epidermis. These scattered keratinocytes had small, round, pyknotic, blue nuclei with perinuclear clearing and abundant light pink cytoplasm; the histopathologic features were those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. Pagetoid dyskeratosis can be an incidental microscopic finding but has been described as a histopathologic feature in biopsy specimens of orange-brown plaques or hyperpigmented macules from the hands.1Trauma may be an inciting factor. The toe lesions in this patient with pagetoid dyskeratosis were likely analogous to pagetoid dyskeratosis of the hands. Pagetoid dyskeratosis, which was originally thought to be an artifact of processing, is a pattern of reactive premature keratinization that is often considered secondary to trauma or friction; however, its pathophysiologic mechanisms are not completely understood.2A unique feature of pagetoid dyskeratosis is that it is often associated with orthokeratosis rather than parakeratosis, and intercellular bridges with other keratinocytes are maintained.2,3This is in contrast to most dyskeratotic processes, which have dyskeratotic cells showing dense eosinophilic cytoplasm and overlying parakeratosis.3The pattern of pagetoid dyskeratosis can also be incidentally seen in the epidermis of melanocytic nevi, acrochordons, and fibromas, even in the absence of any inciting trauma.3Body sites that are most susceptible to rubbing or friction, such as the axillary region, head, and trunk, show the highest incidence of pagetoid dyskeratosis, which supports the hypothesis of an association with a friction-induced mechanism.2,3Most cases of pagetoid dyskeratosis are self-limiting, without further treatment needed. However, a few case reports indicate that lesions were treated with keratolytics, such as urea- or lactic acid−based creams or cryotherapy, with limited success.4 Although pagetoid dyskeratosis itself is a benign finding, neoplasia must be ruled out. Pagetoid Bowen disease can present clinically as a slow-growing variably pigmented plaque or scaly lesion, often in areas with sun exposure. Under histopathologic examination, the epidermis shows enlarged atypical keratinocytes scattered at all levels of the epidermis, with interspersed mitoses.5The stratum corneum often shows alternating patterns of orthokeratosis and parakeratosis, and dyskeratotic cells are also present. There is a tinctorial difference between atypical cells and surrounding normal keratinocytes.5 Epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV) is an autosomal recessive or acquired condition that is associated with β−human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Lesions vary in appearance, ranging from multiple flat papules resembling verruca plana to pityriasiform, thin plaques, and brown macules; lesions are commonly on the face or distal extremities.6Histopathologically, the epidermis is acanthotic and hyperkeratotic, with an irregular granular layer. The cells have perinuclear halos with blue-gray pale cytoplasm.6EV cells differ greatly morphologically from those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. If testing for HPV is performed (not required for either diagnosis), HPV can be detected in EV but not in pagetoid dyskeratosis. Human polyomaviruses 6 and 7, which are chronically shed from the skin, can cause pruritus and skin thickening in individuals who are immunocompromised. Histopathologic findings include dyskeratotic cells in the epidermis and parakeratotic cells with pink cytoplasm in layers within the stratum corneum, resembling peacock plumage.7 In summary, pagetoid dyskeratosis can be the characteristic microscopic finding in yellow-brown plaques on acral surfaces. Although its exact pathomechanism is unknown, this type of clinical presentation with pagetoid dyskeratosis may be secondary to chronic friction.

case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of yellow-brown plaques on the dorsal bilateral first digits of the feet, with prominent scale and a healing biopsy site on the right great toe. Plaques are centered on the interphalangeal joint, potentially an area of high friction. B, Histopathologic examination showed large cells with small, round, dark blue central nuclei and abundant light pink cytoplasm scattered within the epidermis.
case_info.explanation: The shave biopsy findings revealed numerous keratinocytes with abundant pink cytoplasm, scattered at all levels of the epidermis. These scattered keratinocytes had small, round, pyknotic, blue nuclei with perinuclear clearing and abundant light pink cytoplasm; the histopathologic features were those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. Pagetoid dyskeratosis can be an incidental microscopic finding but has been described as a histopathologic feature in biopsy specimens of orange-brown plaques or hyperpigmented macules from the hands.1Trauma may be an inciting factor. The toe lesions in this patient with pagetoid dyskeratosis were likely analogous to pagetoid dyskeratosis of the hands. Pagetoid dyskeratosis, which was originally thought to be an artifact of processing, is a pattern of reactive premature keratinization that is often considered secondary to trauma or friction; however, its pathophysiologic mechanisms are not completely understood.2A unique feature of pagetoid dyskeratosis is that it is often associated with orthokeratosis rather than parakeratosis, and intercellular bridges with other keratinocytes are maintained.2,3This is in contrast to most dyskeratotic processes, which have dyskeratotic cells showing dense eosinophilic cytoplasm and overlying parakeratosis.3The pattern of pagetoid dyskeratosis can also be incidentally seen in the epidermis of melanocytic nevi, acrochordons, and fibromas, even in the absence of any inciting trauma.3Body sites that are most susceptible to rubbing or friction, such as the axillary region, head, and trunk, show the highest incidence of pagetoid dyskeratosis, which supports the hypothesis of an association with a friction-induced mechanism.2,3Most cases of pagetoid dyskeratosis are self-limiting, without further treatment needed. However, a few case reports indicate that lesions were treated with keratolytics, such as urea- or lactic acid−based creams or cryotherapy, with limited success.4 Although pagetoid dyskeratosis itself is a benign finding, neoplasia must be ruled out. Pagetoid Bowen disease can present clinically as a slow-growing variably pigmented plaque or scaly lesion, often in areas with sun exposure. Under histopathologic examination, the epidermis shows enlarged atypical keratinocytes scattered at all levels of the epidermis, with interspersed mitoses.5The stratum corneum often shows alternating patterns of orthokeratosis and parakeratosis, and dyskeratotic cells are also present. There is a tinctorial difference between atypical cells and surrounding normal keratinocytes.5 Epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV) is an autosomal recessive or acquired condition that is associated with β−human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Lesions vary in appearance, ranging from multiple flat papules resembling verruca plana to pityriasiform, thin plaques, and brown macules; lesions are commonly on the face or distal extremities.6Histopathologically, the epidermis is acanthotic and hyperkeratotic, with an irregular granular layer. The cells have perinuclear halos with blue-gray pale cytoplasm.6EV cells differ greatly morphologically from those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. If testing for HPV is performed (not required for either diagnosis), HPV can be detected in EV but not in pagetoid dyskeratosis. Human polyomaviruses 6 and 7, which are chronically shed from the skin, can cause pruritus and skin thickening in individuals who are immunocompromised. Histopathologic findings include dyskeratotic cells in the epidermis and parakeratotic cells with pink cytoplasm in layers within the stratum corneum, resembling peacock plumage.7 In summary, pagetoid dyskeratosis can be the characteristic microscopic finding in yellow-brown plaques on acral surfaces. Although its exact pathomechanism is unknown, this type of clinical presentation with pagetoid dyskeratosis may be secondary to chronic friction.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.scenario: A man in his 30s presented with an approximately 6-month history of asymptomatic plaques on the dorsal bilateral first digits of the feet. He had no relevant medical history or any known inciting factors. Physical examination demonstrated thick yellow to brown plaques overlying the interphalangeal joints of both first digits of the feet (Figure, A). A combination of urea cream, 20%, and clobetasol ointment, 0.05%, applied twice daily to the affected area for approximately 4 weeks yielded no improvement. case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of yellow-brown plaques on the dorsal bilateral first digits of the feet, with prominent scale and a healing biopsy site on the right great toe. Plaques are centered on the interphalangeal joint, potentially an area of high friction. B, Histopathologic examination showed large cells with small, round, dark blue central nuclei and abundant light pink cytoplasm scattered within the epidermis.
case_info.explanation: The shave biopsy findings revealed numerous keratinocytes with abundant pink cytoplasm, scattered at all levels of the epidermis. These scattered keratinocytes had small, round, pyknotic, blue nuclei with perinuclear clearing and abundant light pink cytoplasm; the histopathologic features were those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. Pagetoid dyskeratosis can be an incidental microscopic finding but has been described as a histopathologic feature in biopsy specimens of orange-brown plaques or hyperpigmented macules from the hands.1Trauma may be an inciting factor. The toe lesions in this patient with pagetoid dyskeratosis were likely analogous to pagetoid dyskeratosis of the hands. Pagetoid dyskeratosis, which was originally thought to be an artifact of processing, is a pattern of reactive premature keratinization that is often considered secondary to trauma or friction; however, its pathophysiologic mechanisms are not completely understood.2A unique feature of pagetoid dyskeratosis is that it is often associated with orthokeratosis rather than parakeratosis, and intercellular bridges with other keratinocytes are maintained.2,3This is in contrast to most dyskeratotic processes, which have dyskeratotic cells showing dense eosinophilic cytoplasm and overlying parakeratosis.3The pattern of pagetoid dyskeratosis can also be incidentally seen in the epidermis of melanocytic nevi, acrochordons, and fibromas, even in the absence of any inciting trauma.3Body sites that are most susceptible to rubbing or friction, such as the axillary region, head, and trunk, show the highest incidence of pagetoid dyskeratosis, which supports the hypothesis of an association with a friction-induced mechanism.2,3Most cases of pagetoid dyskeratosis are self-limiting, without further treatment needed. However, a few case reports indicate that lesions were treated with keratolytics, such as urea- or lactic acid−based creams or cryotherapy, with limited success.4 Although pagetoid dyskeratosis itself is a benign finding, neoplasia must be ruled out. Pagetoid Bowen disease can present clinically as a slow-growing variably pigmented plaque or scaly lesion, often in areas with sun exposure. Under histopathologic examination, the epidermis shows enlarged atypical keratinocytes scattered at all levels of the epidermis, with interspersed mitoses.5The stratum corneum often shows alternating patterns of orthokeratosis and parakeratosis, and dyskeratotic cells are also present. There is a tinctorial difference between atypical cells and surrounding normal keratinocytes.5 Epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV) is an autosomal recessive or acquired condition that is associated with β−human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Lesions vary in appearance, ranging from multiple flat papules resembling verruca plana to pityriasiform, thin plaques, and brown macules; lesions are commonly on the face or distal extremities.6Histopathologically, the epidermis is acanthotic and hyperkeratotic, with an irregular granular layer. The cells have perinuclear halos with blue-gray pale cytoplasm.6EV cells differ greatly morphologically from those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. If testing for HPV is performed (not required for either diagnosis), HPV can be detected in EV but not in pagetoid dyskeratosis. Human polyomaviruses 6 and 7, which are chronically shed from the skin, can cause pruritus and skin thickening in individuals who are immunocompromised. Histopathologic findings include dyskeratotic cells in the epidermis and parakeratotic cells with pink cytoplasm in layers within the stratum corneum, resembling peacock plumage.7 In summary, pagetoid dyskeratosis can be the characteristic microscopic finding in yellow-brown plaques on acral surfaces. case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of yellow-brown plaques on the dorsal bilateral first digits of the feet, with prominent scale and a healing biopsy site on the right great toe. Plaques are centered on the interphalangeal joint, potentially an area of high friction. B, Histopathologic examination showed large cells with small, round, dark blue central nuclei and abundant light pink cytoplasm scattered within the epidermis.
case_info.explanation: The shave biopsy findings revealed numerous keratinocytes with abundant pink cytoplasm, scattered at all levels of the epidermis. These scattered keratinocytes had small, round, pyknotic, blue nuclei with perinuclear clearing and abundant light pink cytoplasm; the histopathologic features were those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. Pagetoid dyskeratosis can be an incidental microscopic finding but has been described as a histopathologic feature in biopsy specimens of orange-brown plaques or hyperpigmented macules from the hands.1Trauma may be an inciting factor. The toe lesions in this patient with pagetoid dyskeratosis were likely analogous to pagetoid dyskeratosis of the hands. Pagetoid dyskeratosis, which was originally thought to be an artifact of processing, is a pattern of reactive premature keratinization that is often considered secondary to trauma or friction; however, its pathophysiologic mechanisms are not completely understood.2A unique feature of pagetoid dyskeratosis is that it is often associated with orthokeratosis rather than parakeratosis, and intercellular bridges with other keratinocytes are maintained.2,3This is in contrast to most dyskeratotic processes, which have dyskeratotic cells showing dense eosinophilic cytoplasm and overlying parakeratosis.3The pattern of pagetoid dyskeratosis can also be incidentally seen in the epidermis of melanocytic nevi, acrochordons, and fibromas, even in the absence of any inciting trauma.3Body sites that are most susceptible to rubbing or friction, such as the axillary region, head, and trunk, show the highest incidence of pagetoid dyskeratosis, which supports the hypothesis of an association with a friction-induced mechanism.2,3Most cases of pagetoid dyskeratosis are self-limiting, without further treatment needed. However, a few case reports indicate that lesions were treated with keratolytics, such as urea- or lactic acid−based creams or cryotherapy, with limited success.4 Although pagetoid dyskeratosis itself is a benign finding, neoplasia must be ruled out. Pagetoid Bowen disease can present clinically as a slow-growing variably pigmented plaque or scaly lesion, often in areas with sun exposure. Under histopathologic examination, the epidermis shows enlarged atypical keratinocytes scattered at all levels of the epidermis, with interspersed mitoses.5The stratum corneum often shows alternating patterns of orthokeratosis and parakeratosis, and dyskeratotic cells are also present. There is a tinctorial difference between atypical cells and surrounding normal keratinocytes.5 Epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV) is an autosomal recessive or acquired condition that is associated with β−human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Lesions vary in appearance, ranging from multiple flat papules resembling verruca plana to pityriasiform, thin plaques, and brown macules; lesions are commonly on the face or distal extremities.6Histopathologically, the epidermis is acanthotic and hyperkeratotic, with an irregular granular layer. The cells have perinuclear halos with blue-gray pale cytoplasm.6EV cells differ greatly morphologically from those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. If testing for HPV is performed (not required for either diagnosis), HPV can be detected in EV but not in pagetoid dyskeratosis. Human polyomaviruses 6 and 7, which are chronically shed from the skin, can cause pruritus and skin thickening in individuals who are immunocompromised. Histopathologic findings include dyskeratotic cells in the epidermis and parakeratotic cells with pink cytoplasm in layers within the stratum corneum, resembling peacock plumage.7 In summary, pagetoid dyskeratosis can be the characteristic microscopic finding in yellow-brown plaques on acral surfaces. Although its exact pathomechanism is unknown, this type of clinical presentation with pagetoid dyskeratosis may be secondary to chronic friction.

case_info.scenario: A man in his 30s presented with an approximately 6-month history of asymptomatic plaques on the dorsal bilateral first digits of the feet. He had no relevant medical history or any known inciting factors. Physical examination demonstrated thick yellow to brown plaques overlying the interphalangeal joints of both first digits of the feet (Figure, A). A combination of urea cream, 20%, and clobetasol ointment, 0.05%, applied twice daily to the affected area for approximately 4 weeks yielded no improvement. At a follow-up visit, a tangential shave biopsy specimen was taken from the right dorsal first digit toe (Figure, B).
case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of yellow-brown plaques on the dorsal bilateral first digits of the feet, with prominent scale and a healing biopsy site on the right great toe. Plaques are centered on the interphalangeal joint, potentially an area of high friction. B, Histopathologic examination showed large cells with small, round, dark blue central nuclei and abundant light pink cytoplasm scattered within the epidermis.
case_info.explanation: The shave biopsy findings revealed numerous keratinocytes with abundant pink cytoplasm, scattered at all levels of the epidermis. These scattered keratinocytes had small, round, pyknotic, blue nuclei with perinuclear clearing and abundant light pink cytoplasm; the histopathologic features were those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. Pagetoid dyskeratosis can be an incidental microscopic finding but has been described as a histopathologic feature in biopsy specimens of orange-brown plaques or hyperpigmented macules from the hands.1Trauma may be an inciting factor. The toe lesions in this patient with pagetoid dyskeratosis were likely analogous to pagetoid dyskeratosis of the hands. Pagetoid dyskeratosis, which was originally thought to be an artifact of processing, is a pattern of reactive premature keratinization that is often considered secondary to trauma or friction; however, its pathophysiologic mechanisms are not completely understood.2A unique feature of pagetoid dyskeratosis is that it is often associated with orthokeratosis rather than parakeratosis, and intercellular bridges with other keratinocytes are maintained.2,3This is in contrast to most dyskeratotic processes, which have dyskeratotic cells showing dense eosinophilic cytoplasm and overlying parakeratosis.3The pattern of pagetoid dyskeratosis can also be incidentally seen in the epidermis of melanocytic nevi, acrochordons, and fibromas, even in the absence of any inciting trauma.3Body sites that are most susceptible to rubbing or friction, such as the axillary region, head, and trunk, show the highest incidence of pagetoid dyskeratosis, which supports the hypothesis of an association with a friction-induced mechanism.2,3Most cases of pagetoid dyskeratosis are self-limiting, without further treatment needed. However, a few case reports indicate that lesions were treated with keratolytics, such as urea- or lactic acid−based creams or cryotherapy, with limited success.4 Although pagetoid dyskeratosis itself is a benign finding, neoplasia must be ruled out. Pagetoid Bowen disease can present clinically as a slow-growing variably pigmented plaque or scaly lesion, often in areas with sun exposure. Under histopathologic examination, the epidermis shows enlarged atypical keratinocytes scattered at all levels of the epidermis, with interspersed mitoses.5The stratum corneum often shows alternating patterns of orthokeratosis and parakeratosis, and dyskeratotic cells are also present. There is a tinctorial difference between atypical cells and surrounding normal keratinocytes.5 Epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV) is an autosomal recessive or acquired condition that is associated with β−human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Lesions vary in appearance, ranging from multiple flat papules resembling verruca plana to pityriasiform, thin plaques, and brown macules; lesions are commonly on the face or distal extremities.6Histopathologically, the epidermis is acanthotic and hyperkeratotic, with an irregular granular layer. The cells have perinuclear halos with blue-gray pale cytoplasm.6EV cells differ greatly morphologically from those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. If testing for HPV is performed (not required for either diagnosis), HPV can be detected in EV but not in pagetoid dyskeratosis. Human polyomaviruses 6 and 7, which are chronically shed from the skin, can cause pruritus and skin thickening in individuals who are immunocompromised. Histopathologic findings include dyskeratotic cells in the epidermis and parakeratotic cells with pink cytoplasm in layers within the stratum corneum, resembling peacock plumage.7 In summary, pagetoid dyskeratosis can be the characteristic microscopic finding in yellow-brown plaques on acral surfaces. Although its exact pathomechanism is unknown, this type of clinical presentation with pagetoid dyskeratosis may be secondary to chronic friction.

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting

       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an

   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

Case:

He had no relevant medical history or any known inciting factors. Physical examination demonstrated thick yellow to brown plaques overlying the interphalangeal joints of both first digits of the feet (Figure, A). At a follow-up visit, a tangential shave biopsy specimen was taken from the right dorsal first digit toe (Figure, B).

The goal is to address the underlying dyskeratosis, and while topical treatments have failed, considering alternative therapies or a more aggressive approach may be warranted to manage the condition effectively.

I still believe this diagnosis fits the clinical and histopathological findings effectively.
[AI Assistant]: Your point about chronic irritation leading to clinical plaques is important, but Pagetoid dyskeratosis is a histological finding of isolated, scattered cells, not a proliferative process that forms thick plaques. The biopsy shows sheets of these cells forming a mass, which is inconsistent with an incidental finding. I am still inclined towards Pagetoid dyskeratosis, but I acknowledge the need to remain open to considering other possibilities if the clinical course does not evolve as expected. Could you elaborate on how you would differentiate between the options, particularly between Pagetoid dyskeratosis and Bowen disease in this context?

Bowen disease (squamous cell carcinoma in situ) shows a full-thickness proliferation of atypical keratinocytes, forming a discrete, persistent plaque exactly as described, which is why it is the diagnosis here.
[Doctor]: Your distinction between Pagetoid dyskeratosis and Bowen disease is insightful, and I can see how the latter aligns more closely with the features of a persistent, treatment-resistant plaque. The description of full-thickness atypical keratinocyte proliferation in Bowen disease does indeed match the findings we would expect from the biopsy. I acknowledge that this could be a more fitting diagnosis in light of the clinical persistence and characteristics displayed. Therefore, I am willing to shift my consideration towards Bowen disease as the primary diagnosis for this case.
[AI Assistant]: I agree; your shift to Bowen disease is correct. The combination of a chronic, asymptomatic plaque unresponsive to potent topical steroids and the histologic description of a full-thickness proliferation of atypical keratinocytes is classic for squamous cell carcinoma in situ. The case is now resolved with this diagnosis.

case_info.scenario: A man in his 30s presented with an approximately 6-month history of asymptomatic plaques on the dorsal bilateral first digits of the feet. He had no relevant medical history or any known inciting factors. Physical examination demonstrated thick yellow to brown plaques overlying the interphalangeal joints of both first digits of the feet (Figure, A). A combination of urea cream, 20%, and clobetasol ointment, 0.05%, applied twice daily to the affected area for approximately 4 weeks yielded no improvement. At a follow-up visit, a tangential shave biopsy specimen was taken from the right dorsal first digit toe (Figure, B).
case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of yellow-brown plaques on the dorsal bilateral first digits of the feet, with prominent scale and a healing biopsy site on the right great toe. Plaques are centered on the interphalangeal joint, potentially an area of high friction. B, Histopathologic examination showed large cells with small, round, dark blue central nuclei and abundant light pink cytoplasm scattered within the epidermis.
case_info.explanation: The shave biopsy findings revealed numerous keratinocytes with abundant pink cytoplasm, scattered at all levels of the epidermis. These scattered keratinocytes had small, round, pyknotic, blue nuclei with perinuclear clearing and abundant light pink cytoplasm; the histopathologic features were those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. Pagetoid dyskeratosis can be an incidental microscopic finding but has been described as a histopathologic feature in biopsy specimens of orange-brown plaques or hyperpigmented macules from the hands.1Trauma may be an inciting factor. The toe lesions in this patient with pagetoid dyskeratosis were likely analogous to pagetoid dyskeratosis of the hands. Pagetoid dyskeratosis, which was originally thought to be an artifact of processing, is a pattern of reactive premature keratinization that is often considered secondary to trauma or friction; however, its pathophysiologic mechanisms are not completely understood.2A unique feature of pagetoid dyskeratosis is that it is often associated with orthokeratosis rather than parakeratosis, and intercellular bridges with other keratinocytes are maintained.2,3This is in contrast to most dyskeratotic processes, which have dyskeratotic cells showing dense eosinophilic cytoplasm and overlying parakeratosis.3The pattern of pagetoid dyskeratosis can also be incidentally seen in the epidermis of melanocytic nevi, acrochordons, and fibromas, even in the absence of any inciting trauma.3Body sites that are most susceptible to rubbing or friction, such as the axillary region, head, and trunk, show the highest incidence of pagetoid dyskeratosis, which supports the hypothesis of an association with a friction-induced mechanism.2,3Most cases of pagetoid dyskeratosis are self-limiting, without further treatment needed. However, a few case reports indicate that lesions were treated with keratolytics, such as urea- or lactic acid−based creams or cryotherapy, with limited success.4 Although pagetoid dyskeratosis itself is a benign finding, neoplasia must be ruled out. Pagetoid Bowen disease can present clinically as a slow-growing variably pigmented plaque or scaly lesion, often in areas with sun exposure. Under histopathologic examination, the epidermis shows enlarged atypical keratinocytes scattered at all levels of the epidermis, with interspersed mitoses.5The stratum corneum often shows alternating patterns of orthokeratosis and parakeratosis, and dyskeratotic cells are also present. There is a tinctorial difference between atypical cells and surrounding normal keratinocytes.5 Epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV) is an autosomal recessive or acquired condition that is associated with β−human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Lesions vary in appearance, ranging from multiple flat papules resembling verruca plana to pityriasiform, thin plaques, and brown macules; lesions are commonly on the face or distal extremities.6Histopathologically, the epidermis is acanthotic and hyperkeratotic, with an irregular granular layer. The cells have perinuclear halos with blue-gray pale cytoplasm.6EV cells differ greatly morphologically from those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. If testing for HPV is performed (not required for either diagnosis), HPV can be detected in EV but not in pagetoid dyskeratosis. Human polyomaviruses 6 and 7, which are chronically shed from the skin, can cause pruritus and skin thickening in individuals who are immunocompromised. Histopathologic findings include dyskeratotic cells in the epidermis and parakeratotic cells with pink cytoplasm in layers within the stratum corneum, resembling peacock plumage.7 In summary, pagetoid dyskeratosis can be the characteristic microscopic finding in yellow-brown plaques on acral surfaces. Although its exact pathomechanism is unknown, this type of clinical presentation with pagetoid dyskeratosis may be secondary to chronic friction.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.scenario: A man in his 30s presented with an approximately 6-month history of asymptomatic plaques on the dorsal bilateral first digits of the feet. He had no relevant medical history or any known inciting factors. Physical examination demonstrated thick yellow to brown plaques overlying the interphalangeal joints of both first digits of the feet (Figure, A). A combination of urea cream, 20%, and clobetasol ointment, 0.05%, applied twice daily to the affected area for approximately 4 weeks yielded no improvement. At a follow-up visit, a tangential shave biopsy specimen was taken from the right dorsal first digit toe (Figure, B).
case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of yellow-brown plaques on the dorsal bilateral first digits of the feet, with prominent scale and a healing biopsy site on the right great toe. Plaques are centered on the interphalangeal joint, potentially an area of high friction. B, Histopathologic examination showed large cells with small, round, dark blue central nuclei and abundant light pink cytoplasm scattered within the epidermis.
case_info.explanation: The shave biopsy findings revealed numerous keratinocytes with abundant pink cytoplasm, scattered at all levels of the epidermis. These scattered keratinocytes had small, round, pyknotic, blue nuclei with perinuclear clearing and abundant light pink cytoplasm; the histopathologic features were those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. Pagetoid dyskeratosis can be an incidental microscopic finding but has been described as a histopathologic feature in biopsy specimens of orange-brown plaques or hyperpigmented macules from the hands.1Trauma may be an inciting factor. The toe lesions in this patient with pagetoid dyskeratosis were likely analogous to pagetoid dyskeratosis of the hands. Pagetoid dyskeratosis, which was originally thought to be an artifact of processing, is a pattern of reactive premature keratinization that is often considered secondary to trauma or friction; however, its pathophysiologic mechanisms are not completely understood.2A unique feature of pagetoid dyskeratosis is that it is often associated with orthokeratosis rather than parakeratosis, and intercellular bridges with other keratinocytes are maintained.2,3This is in contrast to most dyskeratotic processes, which have dyskeratotic cells showing dense eosinophilic cytoplasm and overlying parakeratosis.3The pattern of pagetoid dyskeratosis can also be incidentally seen in the epidermis of melanocytic nevi, acrochordons, and fibromas, even in the absence of any inciting trauma.3Body sites that are most susceptible to rubbing or friction, such as the axillary region, head, and trunk, show the highest incidence of pagetoid dyskeratosis, which supports the hypothesis of an association with a friction-induced mechanism.2,3Most cases of pagetoid dyskeratosis are self-limiting, without further treatment needed. However, a few case reports indicate that lesions were treated with keratolytics, such as urea- or lactic acid−based creams or cryotherapy, with limited success.4 Although pagetoid dyskeratosis itself is a benign finding, neoplasia must be ruled out. Pagetoid Bowen disease can present clinically as a slow-growing variably pigmented plaque or scaly lesion, often in areas with sun exposure. Under histopathologic examination, the epidermis shows enlarged atypical keratinocytes scattered at all levels of the epidermis, with interspersed mitoses.5The stratum corneum often shows alternating patterns of orthokeratosis and parakeratosis, and dyskeratotic cells are also present. There is a tinctorial difference between atypical cells and surrounding normal keratinocytes.5 Epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV) is an autosomal recessive or acquired condition that is associated with β−human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Lesions vary in appearance, ranging from multiple flat papules resembling verruca plana to pityriasiform, thin plaques, and brown macules; lesions are commonly on the face or distal extremities.6Histopathologically, the epidermis is acanthotic and hyperkeratotic, with an irregular granular layer. The cells have perinuclear halos with blue-gray pale cytoplasm.6EV cells differ greatly morphologically from those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. If testing for HPV is performed (not required for either diagnosis), HPV can be detected in EV but not in pagetoid dyskeratosis. Human polyomaviruses 6 and 7, which are chronically shed from the skin, can cause pruritus and skin thickening in individuals who are immunocompromised. Histopathologic findings include dyskeratotic cells in the epidermis and parakeratotic cells with pink cytoplasm in layers within the stratum corneum, resembling peacock plumage.7 In summary, pagetoid dyskeratosis can be the characteristic microscopic finding in yellow-brown plaques on acral surfaces. Although its exact pathomechanism is unknown, this type of clinical presentation with pagetoid dyskeratosis may be secondary to chronic friction.

He had no relevant medical history or any known inciting factors. Physical examination demonstrated thick yellow to brown plaques overlying the interphalangeal joints of both first digits of the feet (Figure, A). case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of yellow-brown plaques on the dorsal bilateral first digits of the feet, with prominent scale and a healing biopsy site on the right great toe. Plaques are centered on the interphalangeal joint, potentially an area of high friction. B, Histopathologic examination showed large cells with small, round, dark blue central nuclei and abundant light pink cytoplasm scattered within the epidermis.
case_info.explanation: The shave biopsy findings revealed numerous keratinocytes with abundant pink cytoplasm, scattered at all levels of the epidermis. These scattered keratinocytes had small, round, pyknotic, blue nuclei with perinuclear clearing and abundant light pink cytoplasm; the histopathologic features were those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. Pagetoid dyskeratosis can be an incidental microscopic finding but has been described as a histopathologic feature in biopsy specimens of orange-brown plaques or hyperpigmented macules from the hands.1Trauma may be an inciting factor. The toe lesions in this patient with pagetoid dyskeratosis were likely analogous to pagetoid dyskeratosis of the hands. Pagetoid dyskeratosis, which was originally thought to be an artifact of processing, is a pattern of reactive premature keratinization that is often considered secondary to trauma or friction; however, its pathophysiologic mechanisms are not completely understood.2A unique feature of pagetoid dyskeratosis is that it is often associated with orthokeratosis rather than parakeratosis, and intercellular bridges with other keratinocytes are maintained.2,3This is in contrast to most dyskeratotic processes, which have dyskeratotic cells showing dense eosinophilic cytoplasm and overlying parakeratosis.3The pattern of pagetoid dyskeratosis can also be incidentally seen in the epidermis of melanocytic nevi, acrochordons, and fibromas, even in the absence of any inciting trauma.3Body sites that are most susceptible to rubbing or friction, such as the axillary region, head, and trunk, show the highest incidence of pagetoid dyskeratosis, which supports the hypothesis of an association with a friction-induced mechanism.2,3Most cases of pagetoid dyskeratosis are self-limiting, without further treatment needed. However, a few case reports indicate that lesions were treated with keratolytics, such as urea- or lactic acid−based creams or cryotherapy, with limited success.4 Although pagetoid dyskeratosis itself is a benign finding, neoplasia must be ruled out. Pagetoid Bowen disease can present clinically as a slow-growing variably pigmented plaque or scaly lesion, often in areas with sun exposure. Under histopathologic examination, the epidermis shows enlarged atypical keratinocytes scattered at all levels of the epidermis, with interspersed mitoses.5The stratum corneum often shows alternating patterns of orthokeratosis and parakeratosis, and dyskeratotic cells are also present. There is a tinctorial difference between atypical cells and surrounding normal keratinocytes.5 Epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV) is an autosomal recessive or acquired condition that is associated with β−human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Lesions vary in appearance, ranging from multiple flat papules resembling verruca plana to pityriasiform, thin plaques, and brown macules; lesions are commonly on the face or distal extremities.6Histopathologically, the epidermis is acanthotic and hyperkeratotic, with an irregular granular layer. The cells have perinuclear halos with blue-gray pale cytoplasm.6EV cells differ greatly morphologically from those of pagetoid dyskeratosis. If testing for HPV is performed (not required for either diagnosis), HPV can be detected in EV but not in pagetoid dyskeratosis. Human polyomaviruses 6 and 7, which are chronically shed from the skin, can cause pruritus and skin thickening in individuals who are immunocompromised. Histopathologic findings include dyskeratotic cells in the epidermis and parakeratotic cells with pink cytoplasm in layers within the stratum corneum, resembling peacock plumage.7 In summary, pagetoid dyskeratosis can be the characteristic microscopic finding in yellow-brown plaques on acral surfaces. Although its exact pathomechanism is unknown, this type of clinical presentation with pagetoid dyskeratosis may be secondary to chronic friction.
